svg.aria-label: Diagram: how an Amazon EBS snapshot chain stores data and what deleting a snapshot actually frees, using AWS's own worked example. A snapshot is described two ways on the same documentation page and both are true: it is an incremental backup saving only the blocks changed since the most recent snapshot, and each snapshot contains all of the information needed to restore the data to a new volume. In state one, Snap A is the first snapshot of a volume holding 10 GiB, so it is a full snapshot and 10 GiB is billed. In state two, 4 GiB has changed, so Snap B stores only those 4 GiB and references the unchanged 6 GiB already in Snap A, making the bill 14 GiB. In state three, Snap A is deleted: the 6 GiB still referenced by Snap B is retained and reassigned to Snap B, only the 4 GiB unique to Snap A is removed, and the bill falls to 10 GiB. Deleting a 10 GiB snapshot therefore recovered 4 GiB, and AWS states that costs associated with referenced data are allocated to the later snapshot. The diagram also lists three documented ways an incremental snapshot becomes a full one: a volume encrypted with a different KMS key, a snapshot shared from another account, and archiving, which converts an incremental snapshot to a full snapshot. Finally it notes that Recycle Bin charges nothing for the feature while snapshots in the bin are billed at the same rate as regular snapshots, for a retention period of 1 to 365 days, and that Region-level retention rules apply even to untagged resources.
svg.title: A snapshot is a complete restore point made of partial storage
svg.text: Logically complete. Physically shared. Both sentences are AWS’s.
“save only the blocks … that have changed” · “Each snapshot contains all of the information that is needed to restore”
AWS’s worked example — a 10 GiB volume, two snapshots
STATE 1 — Snap A, full
stores 10 · billed 10 GiB
STATE 2 — Snap B, incremental
stores 4 + refs 6 · billed 14 GiB
STATE 3 — Snap A deleted
6 kept, moves to B · billed 10 GiB
You deleted a 10 GiB snapshot and recovered 4 GiB.
“The 4 GiB of unique data in Snap A is deleted since it is no longer referenced by other snapshots.”
“costs associated with the referenced data are allocated to the later snapshot” — the cost moved, it did not go.
Deleting files from the volume shrinks nothing that already exists
“the data is still considered to be unique data of the earlier snapshots” — and has just become unique to them.
Three documented ways an incremental becomes a full snapshot
1. A different KMS key: “if Vol 2 was encrypted with a different KMS key than Vol 1, then Snap B would be a
full snapshot” — so a key rotation resets the chain, at full price, in one billing period.
2. A source snapshot shared from another account.
3. Archiving: “converted to a full snapshot that includes all of the blocks written to the volume”.
Recycle Bin — the feature is free, the retention is not
“There are no additional charges for using Recycle Bin and retention rules.”
“Snapshots in the Recycle Bin are billed at the same rate as regular snapshots in your account.”
1–365 days for snapshots, and a Region-level rule applies “even if the resources are not tagged”.
Prune from the oldest end, and measure rather than estimate.
Nothing breaks: “you need to retain only the most recent snapshot in order to create volumes”. The oldest
snapshot is simply where unique data concentrates.
